extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (primary); patent applicants and practitioners (secondary)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining and construing means‑(or step‑)plus‑function claim limitations under 35 U.S.C. §112, sixth paragraph and related §112, second and first paragraph issues, with emphasis on computer‑implemented functions, corresponding structure (including algorithms), linking in the specification, rejections, and prior‑art equivalence analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corresponding structure for computer‑implemented means‑plus‑function
rubrics_metrics.description: The corresponding structure for a computer‑implemented function is required to be more than simply a general purpose computer or microprocessor; the structure must include the algorithm needed to transform the general purpose computer or microprocessor into a special purpose computer to perform the disclosed algorithm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Aristocrat, Finisar, WMS Gaming: an algorithm may be expressed in any understandable terms (mathematical formula, prose, flow chart, or “in any other manner that provides sufficient structure”). Not required to list source code or highly detailed description, but must at least disclose the algorithm that transforms the general purpose processor into a special purpose computer programmed to perform the algorithm.

rubrics_metrics.name: 112 second paragraph rejection where no algorithm is disclosed for computer/microprocessor
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph is appropriate if the specification discloses no corresponding algorithm associated with a computer or microprocessor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere reference to a general purpose computer with appropriate programming without explanation, or simply reciting “software,” or mere references to a specialized computer name, undefined computer component (e.g., “access control manager”), “logic,” or “code,” or other black‑box elements are insufficient. See Aristocrat, Finisar, Blackboard, NetMoneyIN, Rodriguez for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: One skilled in the art does not excuse disclosure of algorithm
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that one of ordinary skill in the art could write software to perform the claimed function does not relieve the patentee of the duty to disclose sufficient structure (i.e., the algorithm) in the specification to support means‑plus‑function claim terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Blackboard, Biomedino, Atmel. Examiners should not accept arguments that POSITA knowledge supplants the required disclosure of corresponding structure/algorithm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of algorithm disclosure judged in view of ordinary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification explicitly discloses an algorithm, the sufficiency of that disclosure must be determined in light of the level of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should determine whether one skilled in the art would know how to program the computer to perform the described steps (enablement) and whether the inventor was in possession (written description). Knowledge of POSITA can clarify how to implement a disclosed algorithm (AllVoice, Intel cases). The specification must disclose an algorithm sufficient for POSITA to implement the claimed function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supporting disclosure must clearly link/associate structure to claimed function
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure disclosed in the written description is the corresponding structure only if the written description or the prosecution history clearly links or associates that structure to the function recited in a means‑plus‑function claim limitation under 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ‘link or associate’ requirement is the quid pro quo for employing §112, sixth paragraph. If POSITA cannot identify what structure/material/acts perform the claimed function from the written description, a 112 second paragraph rejection is appropriate (B. Braun, Med. Instrumentation cases). A bare statement that known techniques can be used is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination procedure when §112, sixth paragraph is invoked
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a limitation is determined to be a means‑plus‑function limitation invoking §112, sixth paragraph, the examiner should determine the claimed function and then review the written description (including drawings, figures, tables, sequence listings) for corresponding structure, material, or acts that perform the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings can provide written description (Vas‑Cath). Corresponding structure cannot rely on material only incorporated by reference or on prior art references; the disclosure must come from the application specification itself. Review disclosure from POSITA perspective (Tech. Licensing, Med. Instrumentation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three common grounds for 112 second paragraph rejection when sixth paragraph invoked
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112, second paragraph may be appropriate when: (1) it is unclear whether a claim limitation invokes §112, sixth paragraph; (2) sixth paragraph is invoked and there is no disclosure or insufficient disclosure of structure/material/acts; and/or (3) sixth paragraph is invoked and the supporting disclosure fails to clearly link or associate the disclosed structure/material/acts to the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If examiner cannot identify corresponding structure/material/acts, make a 112 second paragraph rejection. May issue a requirement for information under 37 C.F.R. 1.105 to require identification; failure to supply leads to rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: If corresponding structure disclosed, claim limited to that structure and equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: If the written description sets forth the corresponding structure/material/acts in compliance with §112, second paragraph, the claim limitation must be construed to cover the corresponding structure/material/acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional limitations not recited in the claim, or structural limitations in the written description unnecessary to perform the claimed function, cannot be imported into the claim (Welker Bearing, Wenger). Examiner should construe means‑plus‑function limitation consistent with disclosed corresponding structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific‑term disclosure versus incorporation by reference
rubrics_metrics.description: (A) If corresponding structure/material/acts are described in the specification in specific terms and one skilled in the art could identify them from that description, then §112, second and sixth paragraphs are satisfied. (B) If described in broad generic terms with specific details incorporated by reference, examiner must review the specification alone (not rely on incorporated document) and determine whether POSITA could identify the corresponding structure; if not, applicant must amend the specification to include only the relevant portions of the referenced document that correspond to the means‑plus‑function limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Atmel, Dossel, Intel. Applicant should not be required to insert entire referenced document—only relevant portions to maintain conciseness. If POSITA can identify structure from spec alone, requirement satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing §112 first paragraph support for means‑plus‑function limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining whether there exists §112, first paragraph support for the claim limitation, the examiner must consider not only the summary and detailed description but also the original claims, abstract, and drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Mott, Anderson, Hill‑Rom, Armbruster, Vas‑Cath, Wolfensperger: all parts of the original disclosure may provide support. Examiner may require applicant to clarify record per 37 C.F.R. 1.75(d) if antecedent basis is not clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. 1.75(d)(1) and the duty to provide antecedent basis/clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The terms and phrases used in the claims must find clear support or antecedent basis in the description so that the meaning of the terms in the claims may be ascertainable by reference to the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the written description only implicitly sets forth corresponding structure/material/acts and POSITA would recognize it, the examiner should either have applicant amend the written description to expressly recite the structure/material/acts or state on the record what structure/material/acts perform the function. The PTO may require explicit antecedent basis even if implicit support exists (B. Braun, Wolfensperger).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single means claims and enablement (Donaldson/Hyatt guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Donaldson does not affect In re Hyatt: a single means claim does not comply with the enablement requirement of §112, first paragraph; Donaldson applies only to limitations drafted to correspond to §112, sixth paragraph (claims to combinations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure the record is clear in Office actions about invocation of §112, sixth paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner should specify in the Office action that a claim limitation has been interpreted under §112, sixth paragraph, and when non‑“means for” language invokes sixth paragraph, explain why (e.g., functional term coupled to non‑structural word such as “module for”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office action may also specify what the specification identifies as the corresponding structure. If corresponding structure is not clearly identifiable, the Office action should attempt to identify the structure most closely associated to facilitate prior art search, especially where implementation mode (hardware vs software) is unclear.

rubrics_metrics.name: On allowance, state sixth paragraph interpretation and associated structure
rubrics_metrics.description: When allowing a claim that was treated under §112, sixth paragraph, the examiner should indicate that the claim was interpreted under §112, sixth paragraph in the reasons for allowance and clarify the associated structure if not previously made of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This should be done if such an explanation has not been previously provided on the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of broadest reasonable interpretation and scope of search (Donaldson)
rubrics_metrics.description: Donaldson reaffirms that claim language should be given its broadest reasonable interpretation; prior art application to a means/step‑plus‑function limitation requires the prior art element perform the identical function specified in the claim. If a prior art reference teaches identity of function, examiner bears initial burden to show the prior art structure is the same as or equivalent to the structure disclosed in the specification as corresponding to the claimed means/step plus function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Donaldson does not substantially alter search practice: examiner must show identity of function and equivalence to identify prior art anticipation or obviousness under means‑plus‑function limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two‑step Golight analysis for construing means‑plus‑function limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: First, define the particular function of the claim limitation (include only limitations contained in the claim language). Second, look to the specification and identify the corresponding structure for that function; structure is “corresponding” only if the specification or prosecution history clearly links or associates that structure to the function recited in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Golight, Budde, Cardiac Pacemakers, Med. Instrumentation & Elekta: exercise care if specification provides a special definition; absent definition, apply judgment to determine scope consistent with specification disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making a prima facie case of equivalence for prior art elements
rubrics_metrics.description: If examiner finds a prior art element (A) performs the claimed function, (B) is not excluded by an explicit definition in the specification for an equivalent, and (C) is an equivalent of the means‑/step‑plus‑function limitation, the examiner should explain and rationalize why the prior art element is an equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors supporting equivalence include: (A) performs identical function in substantially the same way and produces substantially the same results (Kemco, Odetics); (B) POSITA would recognize interchangeability (Caterpillar v. Deere, Al‑Site); (C) insubstantial differences between prior art element and corresponding element in specification (IMS, Warner‑Jenkinson). The overall structure corresponding to the claimed function is what matters; individual components of that overall structure are not claim limitations. Advantages unrelated to claimed function should not be considered in an equivalents determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate obviousness of substitution and shift of burden to applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiner should, where appropriate, demonstrate why it would have been obvious to substitute applicant’s described structure/material/acts for that described in the prior art reference; after the examiner's prima facie showing, the burden shifts to the applicant to show the prior art element is not an equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Brown, In re Mulder, and In re Walter. No further analysis by examiner is required until applicant disputes the equivalence and provides reasons.
